st.headline: Evergrande creditors owed $57 billion now face more complex path
st.teaser: One principle in Chinese law could in theory help, though it is unclear how that will play out in practice.
fullText: China Evergrande Group’s creditors have known for years they will only get pennies on the dollar back in one of the country’s biggest ever liquidations.
Now, getting even just that has become more complex.

A mainland Chinese court sentenced Evergrande founder Hui Ka Yan to life in prison on Aug 20 and ordered that his assets be confiscated. His companies were fined a combined 15.8 billion yuan (S$3 billion).

Evergrande’s liquidators, who said last year that the builder’s debt load totalled some US$45 billion (S$57 billion), have been pursuing Hui’s around US$7.7 billion in assets worldwide as they try to claw back funds.
For offshore creditors, one concern is that some of Hui’s assets could be drawn into Chinese mainland court’s enforcement proceedings.
“The new judgment has made the liquidation the most complicated we’ve ever seen,” said Foreky Wong, a Hong Kong-based insolvency specialist.
“The ruling could make liquidators’ recovery route more challenging, especially towards Hui’s assets as the liquidators have not yet won their case against Hui.”
There is, however, one principle in Chinese law that could in theory help some creditors.
Compensation for losses and debt repayments take priority over fines and asset confiscation in the country.
But it is unclear how that will play out in practice in one of the world’s biggest-ever cross-border corporate debt clean-ups.

“The penalty on Hui could add more uncertainties to how offshore creditors” can go about seeking to recoup some of their money, said Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis. “Once the government gets all Hui’s assets, how it arranges the distribution will depend on its own considerations.”
The developer’s liquidators in Hong Kong declined to comment.

Evergrande, once the country’s largest developer by sales, defaulted on its offshore bonds in late 2021. Following failed restructuring attempts, it received a liquidation order in Hong Kong in 2024, marking a significant escalation in the unravelling of the sector.

The liquidators are also jostling with the authorities in Hong Kong. Earlier this week, a court in the city began hearing arguments on a challenge brought by liquidators to a HK$1 billion (S$162 million) deal that set up a fund to compensate Evergrande’s minority shareholders.
Deloitte had estimated in 2023 that the recovery rate for Evergrande’s dollar notes would be 3.4 per cent on average if the firm was liquidated.
Most of Evergrande’s offshore bonds were little changed after the mainland court’s ruling, indicated below two cents on the dollar, underscoring holders’ slim expectations for recovery.
Hui was taken away by Chinese police in 2023 and held under residential surveillance – a type of police action that falls short of formal detention or arrest.
Apart from a company filing confirming Hui being put under police control, Chinese authorities have remained tight-lipped about his status since then.

In 2024, Chinese regulators accused Evergrande’s main onshore unit of inflating more than 560 billion yuan of revenue by recognising sales in advance, an alleged fraud that dwarfs that of Luckin Coffee and Enron.
China then suspended the operations of PricewaterhouseCoopers, Evergrande’s long-time auditor, for six months and imposed fines.
Much of Hui’s known wealth was derived from his controlling stake in Evergrande and the cash dividends he has received from the company since its 2009 listing in Hong Kong.
Hui had pocketed more than US$7 billion over the past decade, thanks to the firm’s generous payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations. Bloomberg

cna.headline: Asian markets extend rally as traders assess US Treasuries pledge
cna.teaser: Asian markets extend rally as traders assess US Treasuries pledge
fullText: HONG KONG: Asian stocks edged higher on Friday (Aug 21) as investors assessed the US Treasury's move to push down long-term bond yields, while analysts warned that alone would not be enough to keep borrowing costs from spiking.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's pledge that he had more tools to provide support did little to comfort US markets as sceptical Wall Street investors resumed their selling amid concerns over elevated inflation and government borrowing, among other things.
The lack of progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz added to unease on trading floors, with oil prices gradually rising over the past two weeks as the United States and Iran remain deadlocked.

The US Treasury provided a much-needed boost to markets on Wednesday when it said it planned to "at least double" its sovereign bond buybacks, a day after the 30-year yield surged to levels last seen in 2007 just before the global financial crisis.

Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his department had a "big toolkit" to address a rise in yields that it views as unmoored to financial conditions. Such measures could include increased bond purchases beyond the scale announced the day before.
"We think that this is a thinly traded area of the market, that we're in August, and there's been a lot of corporate issuance that's influenced the market," Bessent said.
"We believe that the yields don't reflect the underlying fundamentals."

He added that inflation - which has been running above the Federal Reserve's two per cent target for more than five years - would ease once the United States gets "on the other side" of the Iran war and oil prices retreat.
The increase in yields weighed on Wall Street, where all three main indexes fell as tech firms - which rely on debt to fund their huge investments - dropped.
However, Asia fared better, with tech-rich Seoul helped by a rally in chipmakers Samsung and SK hynix, with the former said to be planning a shareholder return worth as much as US$79 billion.
SK hynix rocketed more than 12 per cent Thursday after announcing a US$29 billion share buyback.
Hong Kong, Singapore, Wellington and Taipei also rose, though Tokyo, Sydney and Shanghai dipped.

On currency markets, the yen rose against the dollar after Japanese inflation picked up last month on higher oil prices caused by the Middle East crisis, giving the country's central bank room to hike interest rates next month.
Observers have said the spike in yields is down to a number of things.

Michael Hewson at MCH Market Insights wrote: "We already knew at the start of this year that governments would be looking to raise a lot of money due to increased spending commitments on both sides of the Atlantic, which would mean that buyers would likely be spoiled for choice.

"With the boom in AI infrastructure spending, we've discovered yet another source of supply in the form of corporate bonds with the likes of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and the like looking to raise up to US$500 billion of their own.
"This excess in supply is also likely an additional factor serving to weigh on global sovereign debt markets with some investors preferring to invest in Big Tech as opposed to indebted sovereigns."
Others pointed to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's refusal to provide markets with forward guidance on the bank's plans as fuelling uncertainty on trading floors.
Traders will be closely watching his speech at next week's annual meeting of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs in Jackson Hole, hoping for some clarification on monetary policy.

listening.title: Singapore Boosts Maritime Defences Amid Regional Chokepoint Pressures
listening.transcript: As geopolitical tensions rise in critical shipping lanes, Singapore is actively working to fortify its maritime defences and logistics infrastructure. Speaking at a maritime forum, the Transport Minister emphasized that global trade flows remain highly susceptible to supply chain bottlenecks. Ensuring the uninterrupted movement of merchant vessels through the Malacca Strait is not just an economic priority, but a security necessity. Consequently, local port operators are embracing next-generation automation to handle sudden spikes in cargo volume.

economistArticle.title: The High Cost of Phantom Tollbooths
paras: For centuries, the world's oceans have functioned as global commons, governed by the foundational principle of freedom of navigation. Yet today, this bedrock of globalization is fracturing under the weight of geopolitical friction and asymmetric threats. From the volatile waters of the Red Sea, where Houthi rebels harass massive cargo vessels, to the strategically sensitive corridors of the South China Sea, global maritime routes are increasingly beset by what can only be described as "phantom tollbooths"—unofficial, unpredictable disruptions that impose heavy economic taxes on the flow of international commerce.

Unlike legitimate customs duties or port fees, which are codified and predictable, these phantom tollbooths manifest as soaring insurance premiums, forced re-routing around the Cape of Good Hope, and protracted shipping delays. The economic toll of these delays is staggering and cascades swiftly through the global supply chain. When shipping companies are compelled to bypass key maritime conduits like the Suez Canal, vessels burn millions of dollars in additional fuel, container turnaround times plummet, and port congestion intensifies. For an island city-state like Singapore, which sits at the nexus of major East-West shipping lanes, these systemic tremors are felt instantly as ships queue in its anchorage, striving to realign their schedules.

What makes this situation particularly insidious is its potential to drive permanent structural inflation. When sea lanes are no longer guaranteed to be open and secure, the cost of moving goods rises permanently, eroding the efficiencies of the globalized division of labor. Central banks, already struggling to stabilize domestic economies, find themselves ill-equipped to combat supply-side shocks generated thousands of miles away at sea. Consequently, nations are starting to reconsider their reliance on distant suppliers, accelerating a retreat toward defensive nearshoring and regional protectionism.

Ultimately, the international community cannot afford to treat the freedom of the seas as a historical luxury that can be compromised during geopolitical standoffs. It is an indivisible public good that requires collective, multilateral defense. If the world allows these phantom tollbooths to become permanent fixtures of the global landscape, the cost will not merely be paid by shipping conglomerates—it will be paid by everyone, in every shop, on every shelf.
economistArticle.cn:
几个世纪以来，世界海洋一直作为全球公域发挥作用，受“航行自由”这一基本原则的约束。然而，如今，这一全球化的基石正在地缘政治摩擦和不对称威胁的重压下发生断裂。从也门胡塞武装袭击大型货轮的红海动荡水域，到战略敏感的南海通道，全球海运航线正日益受到只能被称为“幽灵收费站”的困扰——即对国际贸易流动征收沉重经济税的非官方、不可预测的干扰。

与合法且可预测的关税或港口费不同，这些幽灵收费站表现为飙升的保险费、被迫绕道好望角以及漫长的运输延误。这些延误带来的经济损失是触目惊心的，并迅速在整个全球供应链中产生级联效应。当航运公司被迫绕过苏伊士运河等关键海上通道时，船只要多消耗价值数百万美元的燃料，集装箱周转时间暴跌，港口拥堵加剧。对于坐落在东西方主要航线交汇枢纽的岛国新加坡而言，随着船只在其锚地排队、努力调整日程，这些系统性震荡瞬间便能被感知到。

使这种情况尤为隐蔽和危害深远的，是它有可能推动永久性的结构性通胀。当海运通道的安全和开放不再得到保障时，货物运输成本将永久上升，从而削弱全球化分工的效率。已经在努力稳定国内经济的各国央行，发现自己根本无法应对数千英里外海上产生的供给侧冲击。因此，各国开始重新审视自己对遥远供应商的依赖，加速向防御性的近岸外包和区域保护主义撤退。

归根结底，国际社会不能将海洋自由视为地缘政治对峙期间可以妥协的历史奢侈品。它是一项不可分割的公共利益，需要集体的、多边主义的捍卫。如果世界任由这些“幽灵收费站”成为全球版图上的永久存在，其代价将不仅由航运巨头承担——每家商店里的每一件商品，都将最终由每一个人来买单。

gems.s: For an island city-state like Singapore, which sits at the nexus of major East-West shipping lanes, these systemic tremors are felt instantly as ships queue in its anchorage, striving to realign their schedules.
gems.why: This sentence elegantly uses a non-restrictive relative clause ("which sits...") to introduce geographical context, combined with evocative vocabulary like "systemic tremors" and a vivid parallel structure ("as ships queue... striving to...") to paint a clear picture of economic vulnerability. 句子优雅地运用了非限制性关系从句（"which sits..."）来引入地理背景，结合了诸如“系统性震荡”等形象的词汇，以及生动的平行结构（"as ships queue... striving to..."），清晰地描绘出经济脆弱性的画面。

gems.s: If the world allows these phantom tollbooths to become permanent fixtures of the global landscape, the cost will not merely be paid by shipping conglomerates—it will be paid by everyone, in every shop, on every shelf.
gems.why: This concluding sentence employs a strong conditional 'if' structure coupled with a powerful rhetorical tricolon ("by everyone, in every shop, on every shelf") to build dramatic momentum and emphasize the universal consumer impact of maritime disruptions. 这个结尾句采用了强有力的“如果”条件结构，并结合了极具修辞力量排比（"by everyone, in every shop, on every shelf"），层层递进，强调了海运中断给全球消费者带来的普遍影响。
